title: Normality and character functions on the open Bruhat cell
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $H$ be a reductive $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme], meaning smooth, connected, affine and of finite type, with no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup. Unipotent means unipotent matrices in a faithful representation at geometric points. Fix a split maximal torus $T_H$, a Borel subgroup $B_H$, unipotent radical $U_H$, projection $p_H:B_H\to T_H$, and roots and coroots as in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Write $w_0$ for the Weyl group element reversing the positive roots, choose a representative $n_0\in N_H(T_H)(F)$, and put $C=U_Hn_0B_H$. Here $N_H(T_H)$ is the subgroup normalizing $T_H$, the Weyl group is $N_H(T_H)(F)/T_H(F)$, and $(w\chi)(t)=\chi(n^{-1}tn)$. Multiplication $U_H\times_F B_H\to H$, $(u,b)\mapsto u n_0 b$, is an open immersion with dense image $C$. The coordinate ring $R=F[H]$ is a domain integrally closed in its fraction field $F(H)$ (every element of $F(H)$ satisfying a monic polynomial over $R$ belongs to $R$). Here $F(H)=\mathcal O_{H,\eta}$ is the function field at the generic point [def-sc-function-field]. Restriction embeds $R$ and $\Gamma(C,\mathcal O_C)$ into $F(H)$. For every character $\chi:T_H\to\mathbf G_m$, the formula
$$f_\chi(u n_0 b)=\bigl((w_0\chi)(p_H(b))\bigr)^{-1}$$
defines an invertible regular function on $C$, hence a nonzero element of $F(H)$, with $f_{\chi+\psi}=f_\chi f_\psi$. If $f_\chi$ belongs to $R$, then, under left translation $(a f)(g)=f(a^{-1}g)$, it satisfies
$$u f_\chi=f_\chi,\qquad t f_\chi=\chi(t)f_\chi,\qquad f_\chi(gb)=\bigl((w_0\chi)(p_H(b))\bigr)^{-1}f_\chi(g)$$
for $u\in U_H(A)$, $t\in T_H(A)$, $g\in H(A)$ and $b\in B_H(A)$, for every commutative $F$-algebra $A$. In particular its extension lies in the rational left-translation module $E_{B_H}(w_0\chi)$ defined by this last right-equivariance identity. Rational means a coaction into $V\otimes_F F[H]$ satisfying coassociativity and the counit identity.

source.place: Corollary 1.35 and the smoothness discussion before Proposition 1.26 (integrality and regularity); Theorem 21.73(b), Definition 21.72; proof of Proposition 22.22 and Lemmas 22.23--22.25, pp.469--470. The scheme-level character identities are the displayed calculations in the proof of 22.22.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-bruhat-longest-cell-charts] to $H,T_H,B_H$: its reductivity and algebraically closed field hypotheses are precisely ours. It gives geometric integrality of $H$ and $w_0^2=1$. For the specified representative $n_0$, [lem-sfb-longest-weyl-open-cell] gives the dense open immersion $j:U_H\times_F B_H\to H$, $j(u,b)=un_0b$. Thus every point of $C$ over every $F$-algebra has unique coordinates $(u,b)$. By [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], $B_H=U_H\rtimes T_H$, $p_H$ is a homomorphism with kernel $U_H$ and restriction $1$ on $T_H$. In particular $T_H$ normalizes $U_H$.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 22.22 and Lemma 22.23, printed pp.468–469; scheme-level construction written out.

proof.text: The structure morphism of $H$ is smooth over the field $F$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-scheme-over-field-regular], which has no dimension hypothesis, to see that $H$ is regular and locally Noetherian. Clause (1) of [rem-pc-regular-normal] then makes every $\mathcal O_{H,x}$ an integrally closed domain. No curve-only normality lemma is being used.

Since $H$ is nonempty, integral and affine, [lem-sc-integral-function-field-affine-fraction] identifies $K=F(H)$ with the fraction field of the domain $R=F[H]$. By [lem-sc-integral-scheme-stalks-in-function-field], sections on $H$ and on the nonempty open $C$ inject into $K$, and $K$ is also the fraction field of every $\mathcal O_{H,x}$. Let $z\in K$ satisfy a monic polynomial over $R$. Mapping its coefficients into $\mathcal O_{H,x}$ shows that $z$ is integral over that local ring. Step 2 therefore puts $z$ in its image in $K$, for every $x\in H$. Apply [lem-sc-function-field-sections-glue] with $X=H$ and its open set equal to $H$: it supplies a global section with germ $z$. This is precisely $z\in R$, proving the asserted integral closedness and both restriction embeddings.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 22.22 and Lemma 22.23, printed pp.468–469; scheme-level construction written out.

proof.text: Put $q=(w_0\chi)\circ p_H:B_H\to\mathbf G_m$. Both factors are group-scheme homomorphisms. The morphism $q^{-1}\circ\operatorname{pr}_{B_H}\circ j^{-1}:C\to\mathbf G_m$ is consequently an invertible regular function, with exactly the asserted values $q(b)^{-1}$. Here inversion is inversion in $\mathbf G_m$, not a possible division by a zero section; [def-sc-gm-ga] identifies its coordinate with an invertible Laurent variable. This constructs $f_\chi$. It is nonzero since it is a unit on the nonempty $C$. Addition of characters is pointwise multiplication, so the same construction gives $f_{\chi+\psi}=f_\chi f_\psi$ on $C$ and hence in $K$ by step 3.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 22.22 and Lemma 22.23, printed pp.468–469; scheme-level construction written out.

proof.text:
Compute on $C$, over an arbitrary commutative $F$-algebra. For $v\in U_H$, left multiplication by $v^{-1}$ changes $(u,b)$ to $(v^{-1}u,b)$, so leaves $f_\chi$ fixed. Right multiplication by $b_0\in B_H$ changes $(u,b)$ to $(u,bb_0)$, so multiplies its value by $q(b_0)^{-1}$. For $t\in T_H$, set $s=n_0^{-1}t^{-1}n_0\in T_H$. The identity
$$t^{-1}un_0b=(t^{-1}ut)n_0(sb)$$
is an identity of morphisms, with $t^{-1}ut\in U_H$. Since $p_H(sb)=s p_H(b)$, its value is $q(s)^{-1}f_\chi(un_0b)$. Now
$$q(s)=(w_0\chi)(n_0^{-1}t^{-1}n_0)=\chi(n_0^{-2}t^{-1}n_0^2)=\chi(t)^{-1}.$$
Indeed $w_0^2=1$ from [lem-sfb-bruhat-longest-cell-charts] implies $n_0^2\in T_H(F)$, and the torus is commutative. This gives the weight $\chi$, including the sign and inverse in the statement. The kernel and projection assertions used in these computations are exactly [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure].

source.place: Proof of Proposition 22.22 and Lemma 22.23, printed pp.468–469; scheme-level construction written out.

proof.text: Suppose now $f_\chi\in R$. The three desired identities are equalities of regular functions respectively on $U_H\times_F H$, $T_H\times_F H$, and $H\times_F B_H$. Their restrictions to the corresponding products with $C$ agree by step 5. These restrictions are injective: $C\simeq U_H\times_F B_H$ is affine, since both subgroups are closed in affine $H$. By [lem-sc-integral-scheme-stalks-in-function-field], restriction $R\to S=\Gamma(C,\mathcal O_C)$ is injective (both maps to $K$ agree). The affine-product coordinate formula of [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] identifies each restriction with tensoring $R\to S$ with the coordinate vector space of the other factor. Such tensoring is injective: choose an $F$-basis of that vector space, making the map a direct sum of copies of $R\to S$. Thus the identities hold on the entire products. Evaluating these equal morphisms at $A$-points proves them for every $A$, including nonreduced algebras.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 22.22 and Lemma 22.23, printed pp.468–469; scheme-level construction written out.

proof.text:
For completeness the ambient left-translation action is rational, and restricts to the stated subspace. The coordinate Hopf maps of [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf] give
$$\delta_L:R\to R\otimes_F R,\quad\delta_L(f)(g,a)=f(a^{-1}g).$$
Explicitly, if $\Delta f=\sum f_1\otimes f_2$, then $\delta_L f=\sum f_2\otimes S(f_1)$. The group identities $(ab)^{-1}=b^{-1}a^{-1}$ and $1^{-1}g=g$ yield the coassociativity and counit identities by pullback. Let $\rho_B(f)(g,b)=f(gb)$ and $D(f)=\rho_B(f)-f\otimes q^{-1}$. Then $E=\ker D$ is exactly $E_{B_H}(w_0\chi)$. Left and right translations commute: $a^{-1}(gb)=(a^{-1}g)b$. Pulling this equality back shows that $\delta_L(E)\subseteq\ker(D\otimes1_R)$, with tensor factors reordered. Choose a basis of the last vector space $R$; coefficientwise $D$ vanishes precisely when all coefficients lie in $E$. Hence this kernel is $E\otimes_F R$. The coaction therefore restricts to $E$ and inherits its two identities. Step 6 puts our extended $f_\chi$ in $E$, with the required $U_H$-invariance and $T_H$-weight. No finite-dimensionality or characteristic-zero assumption was used.
